 Hillsborough County dengue response continues as scientists fight endemic status
 BY 
 Jason Fechner 
 Tampa 
 UPDATED 5:59 AM ET Nov. 12, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 4:28 AM ET Nov. 12, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 4:28 AM EST Nov. 12, 2026 
 SHARE 
 HILLSBOROUGH COUNTY, Fla. — The Florida Department of Health is expected to release updated dengue fever numbers Tuesday as Hillsborough County continues working to stop the virus from becoming established locally.
 Last week, dengue cases in Hillsborough County rose from 385 to 407, the highest reported total in the state.
 County officials say the rate of new infections appears to be slowing, and a cold front forecast for this weekend could help reduce mosquito activity. Fewer active mosquitoes could mean fewer bites and a lower chance of dengue transmission.
 However, officials say cooler temperatures alone will not eliminate the virus.
 Hillsborough County has extended its local state of emergency and is continuing mosquito control efforts in partnership with Lee and Manatee counties. Crews have been conducting spray missions during the day and at night.
 This week is expected to be the final week of wide-area aerial spraying using small airplanes at higher altitudes. Helicopter spraying will continue, along with targeted ground efforts in neighborhoods where dengue cases are being reported.
 Josh Bellotti, director of engineering and operations for Hillsborough County, said the county’s goal is not just to reduce the number of cases, but to stop local transmission entirely.
 “We are gonna need to stay on top of it,” Bellotti said. “It’s gonna be all through the winter and into next spring because we want this to not become endemic here like it has in other areas. We really do wanna make sure that we stop this completely, really stamp it out.”
 County officials say they plan to continue mosquito control efforts through at least March.
 If dengue were to become endemic, it would mean that the virus is consistently present in the area. Dengue is already endemic in parts of Southeast Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean.
 For now, Hillsborough County leaders say preventing that outcome remains the focus heading into the winter months.
